verdict: The on-disk fact holds and is now better supported than in the consolidation. The SMDD paper does not say "five partners in total": its only sentence on pairing reads as five random partners per key image, and four later papers repeat that reading, including the organisers' own competition report. The release has five partner images in total per split. The paper's arithmetic (5,000 keys x 5 = 25,000 pairs) fits both readings, so the fair statement is "the release differs from the natural reading of the paper", not "the paper is contradicted" and not "bug". None of the sources I could open reports the property, so it appears new, but only as "to our knowledge": the session's web search budget was already used up, so I could only open pages by known address. Two parts of the consolidated bullet need correcting. First, "no genuine render is a contributor" is the documented design, not a discovery. Second, the idea that SMDD-trained detectors partly detect five faces is untested and partly bounded by the SMDD paper itself: detectors trained on the training split reach 0.42 to 2.51% EER on the evaluation split, which uses five different partners. The rebuild (theme K2) is not found in prior work, but as designed it changes partner count, pair similarity, artefact filtering and tool at once, and the SMDD terms require any derived morphs to be published and shared with the SMDD authors.

verdict: Reject in the current form. Read as an area chair, this is three half-papers that do not support each other. The audit is convincing for one thing only: on FRLL-based diffusion cells, the scores of three released checkpoints move with how the 204 genuine photos were resized and stored (share flagged 5 to 54%, 26 to 51%, 2 to 98%). Every other audit claim is a cue that exists without evidence of use (colour, chroma, the five SMDD partner faces, expression outside CLIP-based networks), an absence result with a failed or missing positive control (GAN), or true only under a class definition the author has not settled (one-photo reconstructions counted as genuine). The method is a landmark-only blending detector. Its target is the Face X-ray map 4·M·(1−M) multiplied by the source difference. Its central argument fails at the pooled score, because noise averaging follows the same dose law as the target. It has no result yet, and by design it is silent on 10 of the 17 benchmark cells, which are the cells where the audit found the problem. The statistics rest on one genuine set of 102 persons shared by all 17 cells, one checkpoint per release, a scoring pipeline that misses the published numbers (5.4 against 1.10; 26.0 against 19.3), and verdict rules written after the data. The fastest ways to change my mind cost CPU minutes to hours: a template and pair-swap control for the map, a same-session two-capture control, a two-by-two of supervision by negatives, and the audit tables redone on the reproducing path under both class policies. Experiments are named in plain words with the ID in brackets, as the author asked. Only one web search ran before the session's shared search budget ran out, so prior-art checks are direct page reads of known papers, not a sweep.

findings.point: Objection 3 (the method's target is already published). The proposed per-patch target is 4·a·(1−a)·|W_A − W_B|. Face X-ray defines the blended image as M·I_F + (1−M)·I_B and its training target as B = 4·M·(1−M), zero for every real image, trained from real images only. The proposal is that map with the mask set to the mixing weight and multiplied by the source difference. Pixel-wise supervision for morph detection was introduced by PW-MAD in 2021 with the same stated motive (less focus on artefacts unrelated to the attack), and the record's own PW-MAD retrain falls under the history control (WebMorph 4.2 to 14.3, AMSL 8.9 to 25.7, MAD22 FaceMorpher 1.2 to 20.7; descriptive, retrain did not reproduce). A frozen CLIP encoder with a light head is UnivFD. Frozen CLIP features with a decoder for manipulation maps is DeCLIP. The second output (re-synthesis evidence) is a generated-image detector of the Aligned Datasets and B-Free kind. Self-blending for morph detection is SelfMAD.

findings.point: Objection 4 (the central argument is wrong at the level of the score). The plan says the target 'cannot be predicted by any property that is constant over an image'. The decision is a pooled scalar and every negative has an all-zero map, so 'global morph flag times an anatomy template' fits the target. Three specific failures. (1) Averaging two captures cuts independent noise variance by the factor (1−a)² + a² = 1 − 2a(1−a). The deficit, 2a(1−a), is exactly half of the target's own factor 4a(1−a): 0.18 against 0.36 at a = 0.1, 0.375 against 0.75 at 0.25, 0.5 against 1.0 at 0.5. A head that reads local noise level therefore reproduces the dose curve and even the spatial shape of the alpha fields, with no ghost or identity content. The negatives W_A and W_B are single captures with full noise, so they do not match this statistic. (2) The ghost-energy target is driven by anatomy (hairline, collar, eye and mouth edges differ for every pair), so a fixed template earns a positive within-image rank correlation; the registered bar of 0.4 has no template baseline, and the code has none. wording_for_paper: At each released detector's own operating threshold, giving the same 204 genuine photos the morphs' resize history raises the share flagged from 5% to 54% (MADation ViT-B/16), from 26% to 51% (MADation ViT-L/14) and from 2% to 98% (SelfMAD), as scored in our pipeline on one released checkpoint each.
All 17 benchmark cells share the same 204 genuine photos of 102 persons. They are not independent replications, and we treat them as one test set.

For expression, colour statistics, chroma subsampling and the five recurring partner faces of SMDD we show that the cue exists in the data. We claim that a detector uses a cue only where a controlled change of that cue moves its scores.

Whether a GAN or diffusion reconstruction of one genuine photo is a genuine image is a policy choice. We report every generator cell under both readings and draw no conclusion that holds under only one.
Where no detector separates morphs from one-identity renders, we report an absence. We call it a failure of the detectors only on sets where a trained probe and an identity oracle succeed.
The blend-evidence map is a detector for landmark morphs. It is not designed to respond to GAN or diffusion morphs, which make up 10 of the 17 benchmark cells.
The map target follows Face X-ray (Li et al., CVPR 2020), with the blending mask replaced by the mixing weight and multiplied by the measured disagreement of the two warped source images.
With 204 genuine photos an equal error rate of 1.0% is two photos. We make no superiority claim on the FRLL FaceMorpher and OpenCV cells.

We do not claim freedom from all shortcuts. We report the score shift under each named benign change, the drop under each planted confound, and the result on one genuine construction that was held out of training.
Statements about SelfMAD and MADation refer to the released checkpoints, not to the methods.

verdict: The package in theme K1 (a dense map whose target is the measured disagreement of the two warped source images, with the morph's own unblended warped halves as genuine images, sold as a way to make image-level benchmark cues unusable) was not found as a whole in any prior work, but none of its three ingredients can be claimed as new without qualification, and my search was cut short (the shared web-search budget ran out after 8 queries, so everything after that was checked by opening known papers directly, not by searching for unknown ones). Ingredient 1, the measured-disagreement target: incremental. It is the face X-ray formula 4M(1-M) of Li et al. multiplied by a difference map of the kind Dang et al. already use as supervision (absolute difference between a fake and its source); algebraically 4a(1-a)|W_A - W_B| equals 4(1-a)|morph - W_A|. No morph detection paper using it was found. Ingredient 2, warped halves as negatives: not found as stated, so new as far as checked, but Seibold et al. (2018) already build partial morphs from morph regions plus "an aligned input image" and train a multiclass stage on "partial morphs with zero ... morphed regions", which read literally is a warped unblended source with an all-zero region label. Ingredient 3, dense supervision as a shortcut blocker: incremental at best. PW-MAD already motivates pixel-wise supervision in this field by "bringing less focus on non-attack-related artifacts", Dong et al. (2023) use local supervision explicitly to stop a global identity shortcut, and Seibold et al. use region labels to stop a detector relying on the eyes alone. What was not found is the explicit argument (an image-constant cue cannot predict a within-image varying target) together with a planted-confound test. That argument, as written in section 3 of the consolidation, is also logically incomplete for morphs blended with one global weight: the target factorises into an image-level factor (zero or not) times a spatial pattern that is largely predictable from visible anatomy, so an image-constant cue can still predict the image-level factor; the protection comes from the matched negatives, not from the dense target. The one unresolved risk is Qin, Peng and Long (TIFS 2022): only its abstract is openly readable, it says a "fine-grained classification loss on the basis of different morphing patterns" that "can locate the local morphed areas", and I could not establish what its label maps are. Until someone reads it, no sentence of the form "first spatially varying supervision in morph detection" is safe; after Seibold et al. it is false anyway at region granularity.

findings.point: Rank 1 of the closest works: Face X-ray (Li et al.) and its descendants LAA-Net and Forensics Adapter. Does: blends two real face images (foreground chosen among the 100 nearest by landmarks), supervises a dense map B = 4*M*(1-M) from the soft blending mask, gives real images an all-zero map, and argues this generalises because it relies only on the blending step. LAA-Net builds heatmaps at the maxima of the same B. Forensics Adapter attaches an adapter to CLIP and trains it with the same boundary map (MSE on 16x16 boundary patches) plus a patch-wise contrastive loss (patch is fake if the forged region covers more than 10% of it), so 'a foundation backbone with a blend-evidence map output' is architecturally its recipe. Does not: use image content in the target (the mask comes from the landmark hull, deformed and blurred); for a morph blended at one global weight a = 0.5 the X-ray is 1 everywhere inside the blended region, so a direct transplant degenerates to a constant map; real negatives are untouched, not warped; no morphs; no argument about image-constant dataset cues, only about 'manipulation-specific artifacts'. Same stated limitation as section 3: 'Our method relies on the existence of a blending step.'

findings.point: Rank 2: Seibold, Samek, Hilsmann, Eisert (2018), morph detection with partial morphs and region labels. Does: builds partial morphs ('some regions are taken from a morphed image and the rest from an aligned input image'; four regions: left eye, right eye, nose, mouth), so one image contains morphed and unblended warped regions; a multiclass pretraining stage has one output per region ('Each class represents one region and if this region is forged, the image belongs to this class') and is trained on 'partial morphs with zero, one, two, three or four morphed regions (each 20%...)'; stated aim is to stop the network relying on one cue ('it might be sufficient to focus on the eyes'; 'force the network to consider all regions'); reports EER 3.1% naive against 2.8% multiclass and robustness to partial morphs of 20% against 87%; observes that the network 'compared different region among each other'. Does not: use dense maps (4 region labels, binary), graded or measured targets, the two halves of each morph as declared genuine images, or any argument about benchmark or file cues. So a target that varies inside the image already exists in morph detection at region granularity, and the 'zero morphed regions' sample is, read literally, a warped unblended source with an all-zero label.

findings.point: Rank 4: dense losses in single-image morph detection whose target carries no more information than the image label: PW-MAD (2021) and SelfMAD++ (2026). PW-MAD: a 14x14 map supervised with 'a label of attack or bona fide for each image pixel', loss 0.5*pixel BCE + 0.5*image BCE; the paper names no source of per-pixel labels and adapts George and Marcel, who state 'we consider all patches have the same label', so the map is the image label repeated. SelfMAD++: LoRA-adapted CLIP plus a convolutional branch 'guided by an auxiliary segmentation module, which acts as a regularizer by disentangling bona fide facial regions from potentially manipulated ones'; in the public code the segmentation target is the binary face-parsing mask for the genuine image and an all-zero map for the simulated morph (mask = cat[raw_mask, zeros_like(raw_mask)]); the self-blend mask is computed and thrown away; loss is cross-entropy on the class plus cross-entropy on the map with weight 1. Its simulated morphs are region-partial self-blends (blend ratio from 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1, 1, 1; 'self-morphing' factor 0.125 to 0.5 inside face-part masks), so region-partial positives exist there too, with image-level meaning only. Neither uses two sources, measured differences, graded maps or warped negatives. SelfMAD++ reports an average EER of 3.91% over nine benchmarks and publishes checkpoints trained on SMDD.

findings.point: Rank 5: Dang, Liu, Stehouwer, Liu, Jain, 'On the Detection of Digital Face Manipulation' (CVPR 2020). Does: supervises an attention map with a measured difference: 'we pair fake images with their corresponding source images, compute the absolute pixel-wise difference in the RGB channels, convert into grayscale, and divide by 255', then 'the threshold of 0.1 to obtain the binary modification map'; 'zero-maps' for real faces and 'one-maps' for entirely synthesised faces. Does not: keep the map continuous, use two sources, weight by mixing, treat morphs, or use processed negatives. This is the precedent for a target measured from the stored source rather than drawn from a mask. For a morph the K1 target is the same quantity up to scale, because morph - W_A = a*(W_B - W_A), so 4a(1-a)|W_A - W_B| = 4(1-a)|morph - W_A|.

findings.point: The central argument in section 3 ('the target cannot be predicted by any property that is constant over an image') does not hold for the target the method now uses. With one global mixing weight, target = c * s(x): c is zero for every negative and positive for every morph, and s(x) = |W_A - W_B| peaks at predictable anatomy (iris, nostril, lip and brow edges, hair outline). A head can learn s(x) from visible content and c from any image-constant cue that separates the classes in training. Only the within-image pattern is protected, not the image score. The first probe AF0 (frozen features, per-patch head) was registered with randomly placed mixing fields (gradients, bumps), for which the argument does hold; its planted-confound falsifier (all mixed images from FRGC pairs, all zero images from colorFERET, tested crossed) therefore tests a different target than the wave-2 design (measured disagreement, uniform weight, halves as negatives). In wave 2 the blocking of unlisted cues is done by the halves, which share source, person, warp, frame and storage with the morph; an image-level classifier trained with the same halves would be protected just as well. The idea generators already named this risk ('anatomy prior times a global morph flag'); it is not yet in the registered falsifiers. A related weakness: AF0's pass mark (within-image rank correlation of predicted and true map at least 0.4) is uninformative for a measured-disagreement target, because the average training map alone will correlate with every true map.

cheapest_decisive_tests: Read Qin, Peng, Long (TIFS 2022), Section III, through an institutional IEEE login (about 20 minutes, no compute). Decide three things: is the feature-wise label constant per image or does it follow a region mask; are splicing or partial morphs with untouched regions trained on; what are the genuine samples. If the label follows a mask, the paper's wording changes from 'first map-supervised morph detector with a varying target' to 'first with a measured, continuous, content-dependent target'.

Read the journal version of Seibold et al. (2018) or its code to settle whether 'partial morphs with zero morphed regions' are warped unblended inputs (about 15 minutes). If yes, the halves-as-negatives ingredient has a 2018 precedent in a pretraining stage and must be cited as such.

Five-arm ablation on the frozen-feature probe setup already built for AF0 (the per-patch head on frozen patch tokens; CPU minutes per head, no new images beyond the stored halves), all with one global mixing weight: (a) image-level label, camera photos as negatives; (b) image-level label, warped halves as negatives; (c) constant map inside the face hull (the face X-ray or PW-MAD style target), halves as negatives; (d) measured-disagreement map, halves as negatives; (e) measured-disagreement map, camera photos only. Train each on the planted-confound set (all morphs from FRGC pairs, all zero-target images from colorFERET) and test on the crossed set. The dense target is a shortcut blocker only if (e) loses at most 0.05 AUC where (a) loses at least 0.20. If (b) holds up as well as (d), the negatives do the work and the claim must be rewritten.

Mean-map baseline (zero compute once targets exist): correlate the average training target map with each held-out true map. Print it beside every predicted-map correlation. If the average map already reaches the registered pass mark of 0.4, the map-correlation check proves nothing about reading local evidence and needs a mean-removed version.

Partner-swap test for the 'global flag times anatomy' failure (CPU minutes): morph the same host A with two partners B1 and B2; per patch, correlate (predicted map for A+B1 minus predicted map for A+B2) with (true map difference), after removing each image's mean. Near zero means the head outputs an anatomy prior scaled by an image-level flag.

Label defence for the halves: share of warped halves W_A that verify against contributor B at a false-match rate of 1 in 1,000 with the face-recognition oracle already used for the twin-validity gate. Near the false-match rate supports 'genuine image of A'; a few percent or more makes it a shape morph and the label needs the author's ruling.

It is the 2026 competitor closest in design, and its dense target is image-constant, so it is the natural 'dense loss without a varying target' comparator.

wording_for_paper: Dense supervision is not new in morph detection. PW-MAD adds a per-pixel loss whose target repeats the image label at every position, SelfMAD++ adds a segmentation branch whose target, in the released code, is the face-region mask for genuine images and an all-zero map for simulated morphs, and Qin et al. supervise feature maps to localise morphed areas [describe their labels after reading the paper]. In the first two the map carries no information beyond the image label.

Seibold et al. trained with partial morphs, in which some facial regions come from a morph and the rest from an aligned source image, and with one output per region, to stop a detector from relying on a single region. We extend this idea from four binary region labels to a continuous per-patch target.

Our target builds on the face X-ray of Li et al., B = 4M(1-M). For a morph blended with one global weight the face X-ray is constant over the blended region and so reduces to a per-image label. We multiply it by the measured local difference between the two warped contributors, so that the target is zero wherever the contributors agree and blending leaves no trace.

Difference maps between a manipulated face and its source are an established localisation target in face forgery detection (Dang et al.). Ours is computed against the warped contributors, which removes the geometric warp from the difference, is kept continuous, and is weighted by the mixing weights; for a morph M = (1-a)W_A + aW_B it equals 4(1-a)|M - W_A|.

We label the two warped but unblended contributors of every morph as genuine images with an all-zero map. This follows the source-paired negatives of self-blending methods, but differs from them in that the geometrically transformed image is itself a genuine sample; in SelfMAD and Self-Blended Images a transformed copy enters only as part of an attack. Pimenta et al. label blends of two photos of one person as bona fide; our negatives contain one photograph only.

The observation that local supervision can reduce reliance on global nuisance information is not ours. PW-MAD motivates pixel-wise supervision by 'bringing less focus on non-attack-related artifacts', and Dong et al. use local artifact supervision to keep a deepfake detector from learning identity. Our contribution is to state the condition under which this holds and to test it with a planted confound: [result].

We do not claim that a dense target alone removes image-level cues. With one global mixing weight the target is the product of an image-level factor and a spatial pattern, and an image-constant cue can still predict the former. In our ablation, [X] of the reduction in cue use comes from the matched negatives and [Y] from the target.

Like the face X-ray, which 'relies on the existence of a blending step', the blend-evidence map is expected to stay silent on GAN and diffusion morphs, which contain no pixel superposition. We report this as a measured limit.

To our knowledge, no prior morph detection method is supervised with the measured disagreement of the two warped contributors. [Use only after Qin et al. has been read in full and the literature search has been rerun.]

Do not write: 'first localisation or dense supervision for morph detection', 'first supervision that varies inside the image', 'PW-MAD follows processing history' (only our non-reproducing re-implementation was tested), or 'the target cannot be predicted by any image-constant property' without the uniform-weight caveat.

verdict: None of the five parts is new as an idea. Each has a published precedent, and the paper is only safe if it says so and claims the narrower thing. (a) One threshold with per-pool false alarms is incremental: NIST FATE MORPH already prints false detection rates for three genuine pools at one threshold per algorithm, and shows resolution effects at equal thresholds. The new parts are paired benign copies of the same photos on the public benchmarks and the worst-pool rule. (b) Null rows are incremental: morph-blind scores are already published on these benchmarks, but as detectors, and the "credit only above the best null" rule has a known logical gap. (c) The ladder is incremental: every rung exists in the morph literature, including same-person "selfmorphs" that Medvedev et al. label bona fide, which is the opposite of the author's ruling. (d) Dose in mixing weight is already done by NIST. Dose in contributor dissimilarity was not found and looks new, but "benchmark construction cannot fake this" is false as written. (e) The neutral-only construction is stated by the dataset authors and its use by detectors was not found in print, so it looks new. But my check of the FRLL files on disk shows the neutral and smiling photo sets differ in background noise in 102 of 102 persons, so the effect cannot yet be called expression, and the project's own registered re-read shows it in one of six MADation releases, with the opposite sign in another. Limit of this check: the shared web search budget ran out after four searches, so every "not found" below rests on direct reading of primary sources I could name and is weak evidence of absence.

wording_for_paper: NIST FATE MORPH reports the false detection rate separately for three genuine pools at each algorithm's threshold, and has shown since 2020 that at equal thresholds false detections fall and misses rise with image resolution. We bring this reporting to the public academic benchmarks and add what a sequestered test cannot publish: paired, benignly processed copies of the same genuine photographs.

On the Greedy-DiM set of the NIST report of 14 September 2026, the two single-image systems with the lowest miss rate at 1% mugshot false detections flag 28.9% and 93.4% of visa photographs at their own thresholds.

Earlier work warned that morph detectors can learn the properties of one pipeline (Scherhag et al. 2020; Spreeuwers et al. 2022; Medvedev et al. 2022). What was missing is a measurement of how much of the reported accuracy on the current public benchmarks this explains.

Following hypothesis-only baselines in language inference and silence-only baselines in spoofing detection, we print scores of models that cannot know what a morph is above each table. A weak null does not show that a cell is free of cues (Feng et al. 2019); we use nulls only to mark cells that cannot measure morph detection.

Each rung of the ladder has a precedent: quality-matched genuine sets (NIST; Scherhag et al. 2020), reconstructed genuine images for GAN morphs (Zhang et al. 2025), and same-person selfmorphs (Borghi et al. 2021; Medvedev et al. 2022, who label them bona fide). Our contribution is to score released detectors on all rungs built from the same host photograph.

NIST reports detector score against the mixing weight. We add a second axis, the dissimilarity of the two contributors, read within strata of gender and photo subset because pairs were selected within those strata.

The benchmark papers state that the Webmorph morphs of MAD22 and all DiM morphs were made from neutral photographs only (Huber et al. 2022; Blasingame and Liu 2024), while half of the 204 genuine photographs are smiling. In the FRLL release the two photo sets also differ in background noise in all 102 persons, so we report a subset effect and separate expression from photo history with a second pool.

verdict: The older record does not contradict the chosen line outright, but it removes three of its comfortable assumptions and shows that several "new" facts were already on file. (a) Every detector in our record that was trained on "same source, differs only by blending" is the most fragile one when genuine photos are softened (the released SelfMAD goes from 2% to 98% of genuine photos flagged; our own patch-token reader on frozen CLIP went from 10.8% to 30.8% false alarms on shrunk photos), and frozen CLIP patch tokens decode the shrink-and-enlarge history at AUC 1.0. Warped halves remove the warp asymmetry the record blamed (the R8 same-person arm), but not the averaging asymmetry. (b) "Frozen" is not what protects: the released frozen-encoder MADation ViT-B/16 rises 6 to 13 points on landmark cells and 21 to 29 points on diffusion cells under the history control, and the frozen-encoder ViT-L/14 release sits at 4.4 / 4.9 / 23.0 / 10.3% on the four landmark cells against the bar of 1.0 / 1.0 / 14.7 / 4.4% set by the adapted release. The record supports a frozen ViT-L/14 only for reading the mixing step of diffusion morphs (four separate experiments), not for a landmark state-of-the-art claim. (c) Transfer to an unseen tool is where our record is worst: training on full-face landmark morphs with their own source photos as the genuine class gave 37 to 52% error on a held-out splice tool until self-blends were added, heads on frozen features trained on one generator inverted on another (0.26 to 0.32), and training on morphs from the very engine AF0 uses made every real MAD22 landmark family worse in the old campaign. On SMDD the rebuild is well supported (five partner faces confirmed here on a second copy, a single sharpness number separates the classes at AUC 0.99 or more, 733 morphs are not square), but the record predicts that a pipeline-matched SMDD costs the MADation recipe its diffusion numbers, and the published morph files cannot carry a ghost-energy target because SMDD's warp factor is random per file. wording_for_paper: In the public SMDD release every attack image in a split shares one of five second contributors (training split: 15,000 morphs, 3,853 first contributors, 5 second contributors), and no genuine image is a contributor to any morph.

A single sharpness statistic (Laplacian variance of the face region) separates SMDD's attack and genuine classes at AUC 0.99 or more; 733 of 15,000 training morphs also differ in image height from every genuine file.

A linear head on a frozen CLIP ViT-L/14 separates diffusion morphs from one-photo reconstructions (0.66 at matched decoding steps) but does not rank two-person morphs above same-person mixes (0.31 to 0.52). We call this reading the mixing step, not reading a second identity.

verdict: The audit's core observation is sound, and I confirmed two of its facts independently: the SMDD five-partner structure (file names on all 30,000 morphs, plus a pixel fit on 300), and the neutral-only composition of MAD22 Webmorph and the DiM families (stated by their own authors). As written, though, a hostile reader from this community can set aside most of the MADation half of the audit and the proposed state-of-the-art bar on one ground: the scores come from our own 512-pixel frames, where published numbers are not reproduced. The gap is larger than the record admits. It is not only MorDIFF 4.9 against 1.10; on FRLL AMSL it is 15.1 against 3.85 and 17.7 against 7.26, and the consolidation's bar (14.7 on AMSL) is twice the published error of the detector it names. The second hard objection is definitional: a one-photo GAN or diffusion reconstruction is not a bona fide image in this community's sense, the author's own 16:00 position leans the same way, and the ladder's verdict words depend on the opposite ruling. Third, the idea itself is in the community's own 2017 guidance (Scherhag et al., co-authored by Busch, Raghavendra, Marcel and Grother), so the novelty is the measurement, and the measurement rests on 204 photos of 102 persons, post hoc, one checkpoint per release, with one failed attempt to generalise to FFHQ. What survives a hostile reading today: the SelfMAD-release results on its own crop that need no class ruling, the file-level construction facts, and the SMDD partner structure as a property of the release with unknown consequence. Order of action: re-score with each release's own crop first, rebase the bar, restructure the claims so the headline needs no class ruling, and write to the author groups today. Web search ran out after four queries, so several standards and prior-work checks are listed as not verified.

The author's own position of 11 Nov, about 16:00, says the same (generated-image detection is a different task; do not penalise morph detectors on it). wording_for_paper: That quality differences between bona fide and morphed samples can bias a detector was stated by the community in 2017 (Scherhag et al., BIOSIG 2017). We measure how far the benchmarks and released detectors in current use depart from that recommendation.

All controlled results use the 204 genuine photos of 102 FRLL persons that every audited benchmark shares, one released checkpoint per method, and decision rules fixed after earlier estimates had been seen. They describe these checkpoints on these benchmarks, not the methods.

Each release is scored with its authors' preprocessing, and our reproduction is printed beside the published value. Where the two differ by more than 1.5 points or 25 percent, the cell is marked 'not reproduced' and we draw no conclusion about the detector from it.

We distinguish three kinds of image: a camera photo with benign processing; a single-identity image that was re-synthesised or blended (a GAN or diffusion reconstruction, a same-person blend); and a morph of two persons. Following NIST, a morph combines two or more individuals. The middle class is reported in its own column and counted neither as bona fide nor as attack.

For the released SelfMAD checkpoint, scored with its own preprocessing, a genuine FRLL photo stored at the size of the published MorDIFF files is flagged in 203 of 204 cases at the benchmark's equal-error threshold.

The released MADation ViT-B/16 checkpoint does not rank two-person diffusion morphs above single-identity reconstructions that were rendered and stored identically (AUC 0.48, 95% interval 0.38 to 0.58; 102 persons; post hoc). [Use only after the own-crop re-score confirms it.]

In the public SMDD release, each of the 15,000 training morphs blends one of 3,853 images with one of five recurring partner images (2,173 to 3,444 morphs per partner); the evaluation split uses five other partners. The SMDD paper describes five randomly chosen partners per key image. Whether detectors use this was not tested here.

In 11 of 17 benchmark cells the morphs are neutral while half of the genuine photos smile. The benchmark authors state this for MAD22 Webmorph and for the DiM families; for FRLL-Morphs it is inferred by an expression probe. We therefore also report every cell with the 102 neutral genuine photos only; one photo is then 0.98 points of BPCER.

Track A uses SMDD as the only morph-detection training data, as MADation and SelfMAD do. Like them it starts from pretrained weights, which the SYN-MAD 2022 rules did not allow. Track B adds real photographs and is not comparable with published SMDD-only results.
We claim the best result only for pixel-blended (landmark) morphs under the size-matched protocol, and we print the native published-protocol table in full, including the cells where we are worse.
For GAN and diffusion morphs we make no detection claim. We report what a separate generated-image output does on them, and how much evidence of a second identity a single image holds.

We could not establish which training epoch the released SelfMAD and MADation checkpoints correspond to, nor whether the SelfMAD release was selected with the public code's default, which picks the checkpoint by test error on FRLL-Morphs, FRGC-Morphs and FERET-Morphs. verdict: Section 3 presents a label convention as physics. The blend-evidence target is zero for one-capture images only because the labels say so; over most of the face, the image trace a head must use to predict it is a loss of fine detail, which denoising or resampling also produces. I measured this in memory on existing landmark-ladder pairs (AR1: FRGC and colorFERET hosts, OpenCV-style engine; nothing written). A two-person morph has 0.52 times the Laplacian variance of its own two warped halves. That one number separates morphs from their own halves at AUC 0.76 at 512 pixels and 0.87 at 224, which is the level of the registered pass marks (0.75 and 0.85). Each target variant has a defect: the mean-absolute-difference map is 74% smooth tone mismatch; the unnormalised patch-deviation map is predicted at rank correlation 0.71 by the image's own local contrast; the registered contrast-normalised map is highest on flat skin (0.97 against 0.73 on eyes and mouth). The target is not small for same-person blends (65 to 76% of the two-person value). Three worries are largely dismissed: about 1% of the disagreement energy lies above what a 224 input can sample, a fixed position template reaches only 0.10 inside the face, and warp size does not change sharpness. The line can survive if the target excludes flat regions, the pass marks move above the sharpness floor, FaceMorpher stops being the deciding tool, and the claim is scoped to studio captures. The identity-shrinkage formula (K6) is correct inside its Gaussian model but is not a ceiling. On exact landmark geometry it predicts 0.94 to 0.99 from genuine photos and I observe 0.82 to 0.85. Fresh within-person variation removes the effect (0.48 to 0.56), a caricature factor of 1.25 removes it (0.55), and two genuine pools differ almost as much as morphs do (0.69 to 0.74).

findings.point: The sentence 'exactly zero for any image made from one capture, whatever its history' is true of the labels, not of the image. Blending two warped faces halves the fine-detail energy, and that cue alone separates a morph from its own unblended halves. So using the halves as negatives does not remove softness, and the claim 'covers cues nobody has listed' cannot stand.

findings.point: The other two target variants are also flawed. The mean-absolute-difference map is mostly smooth tone and lighting mismatch, which leaves no local trace in a blend and which Poisson blending removes. The unnormalised patch-deviation map is predicted by the image's own local contrast, equally well from the unblended half, so within-image rank correlation of 0.4 can be passed by 'local contrast times an image flag'.

findings.point: Splice and Poisson morphs remove most of what the map is trained on. Outside the face there is one contributor, so the target is zero there. Poisson blending re-normalises tone to the host, which is 74% of the mean-absolute target. The closest published precedent lost a factor of seven in error when moving from alpha to Poisson blending. The AMSL cell (bar to beat 14.7% EER) is exactly this case.

Makrushin, Neubert, Dittmann, VISAPP 2017 (checked, PDF pages 41 to 44): the splicing morph has 'a mutual texture, but the geometry is adopted from one of the input faces'; seam smoothed by a Gaussian filter. AMSL dataset page (checked through the fetch tool) says it uses the approach of Neubert et al., IET Biometrics 2018; that paper was not checked.

Score the dense head on it, on the existing Poisson set (H1, A27: 598 MediaPipe-warp Poisson morphs of CASIA look-alike pairs) and on FRLL-Morphs AMSL with history-matched genuine photos. findings.point: The argument 'no property constant over an image predicts the target' does not cover benign processing that varies inside the image and follows the face: burst merging, portrait-mode blur, skin retouching, face-aware sharpening halos, reflections in glasses, flash shadow contours. A phone photo is itself a merge of several frames, so 'one capture' is not a physical category for phone images.
findings.evidence: Hasinoff et al., SIGGRAPH Asia 2016, Google Research page (checked through the fetch tool, abstract only): the system 'captures, aligns, and merges a burst of frames'. For Gaussian patch noise the mean of the top tenth sits 1.75 patch standard deviations above the patch mean, so anything that raises the spread of predictions on a genuine photo (compression, glasses, beard, fringe) raises the image score. The history-shift check was registered for mean pooling only. With CLIP at 224 the hull holds about 69 patches, so the score is the mean of about 7 patches.

(1) A position-only template (leave-one-out mean map) reaches within-image rank correlation 0.10 inside the hull (0.28 over the whole frame; rank-one explained variance 0.02), so a fixed anatomy prior cannot pass the 0.4 learnability mark. Accept a target only if flat is below busy and the contrast correlation is below 0.3 in absolute value. Current values: registered g 0.97 against 0.73 and -0.27; unnormalised deviation +0.71; mean absolute difference 74% tone.

Paired-difference learnability. wording_for_paper: The blend-evidence target is zero by construction for every training image built from one photograph. This is a property of the labels. We do not claim that no single-capture image shows superposition: burst merging, synthetic depth of field, retouching and reflections superimpose content inside one photograph, and we measure false alarms on such variants separately.

Pixel blending of two warped faces halves fine-detail energy (Laplacian variance 0.52 times that of the unblended warped sources in our builds). A detector can therefore separate a morph from its own unblended sources by sharpness alone (AUC 0.76 at 512 pixels, 0.87 at 224). We report all results against sharpness-matched negatives as well.

The target measures disagreement between two captures, not a second identity. A same-person morph carries about 0.7 of the target of a two-person morph, and a photograph blended with its own mirror image carries 0.4 to 0.8.

The map covers pixel-domain blending. Morphs that splice a blended face into one contributor's image, or blend in the gradient domain, retain only the inner-face part of this evidence; we report them as separate cells.
Warp-only images are a control that isolates blending from resampling. They are not counted as genuine photographs when false-alarm rates are reported.

Under a Gaussian model of identity coordinates, a midpoint of two identities has reduced spread, and the best norm test has AUC P(F(d,d) > s). This is a model prediction, not a bound. On exact landmark geometry it overshoots the observed separation by 0.11 to 0.14, the effect vanishes when the midpoint is rescaled by about 1.25, and two genuine photo collections differ by almost as much (AUC 0.69 to 0.74).
